transcript.content: Hello. I'm glad to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

My thoughts jump all over the place and I can’t keep a straight line when I talk or plan anything anymore. It has gotten to the point where I just feel completely overwhelmed trying to do the simplest things.
Have you struggled with these racing thoughts and organization difficulties since you were a child, or is this a relatively new change for you?

This is a relatively new change that started about ten months ago, after I retired early from my museum career to care for my aging mother. I used to be incredibly organized in both my work and my personal life, but now my thoughts are completely disorganized and constantly jumping around.
Have you ever experienced periods lasting at least a few days where you felt unusually energized, hyperactive, or needed much less sleep than usual?

Yes, over the last ten months, I've had stretches of about six months in total where I feel incredibly energized and sleep only two or three hours a night without feeling tired. During those times, I'm buzzing with ideas, racing around the apartment cleaning, and starting huge projects like planning a caregivers' art festival.
Aside from these high-energy times, have you ever experienced periods lasting two weeks or more where you felt extremely down, sad, or lost interest in your usual activities?

Yes, I've had periods, like a long stretch in late summer, where my mood felt completely flat and drained. I lost all interest in things I used to love and would just sit in my robe staring at the wall, barely returning calls from my friends. It was incredibly hard to muster the energy to even shower or cook unless my niece pushed me to do it.
During those high-energy periods, did you ever do things that were risky or out of character, or did they ever lead to hospitalization or serious trouble in your life?

Yes, I did some very risky and out-of-character things, like driving at terrifying speeds on the highway, spending huge chunks of my retirement savings on art supplies and trip tickets, and even meeting up with a stranger from online. I wasn't hospitalized, but these actions were highly unsafe and created serious trouble, leaving me completely unable to manage my own or my mother's appointments. It was all very unlike me and caused a lot of chaos.
How would you describe your mood over the past week or two? Are you currently feeling more down and depressed, unusually high and energized, or perhaps experiencing a mix of both at the same time?

Lately, my mood has been highly unstable and constantly swinging. I fluctuate between feeling bizarrely amped up and almost giddy—where I get easily irritated and snap at people over tiny things—to suddenly feeling completely flat, drained, and just staring at the wall. It really feels like an unpredictable and exhausting mix.
Do these contrasting feelings of being amped up and feeling completely drained happen on the very same day, or even at the same time, and has this been occurring nearly every day?

I'm not entirely sure about them happening on the exact same day or at the same time. It feels more like these states happen in waves or distinct periods, where I'm either very wired and buzzing for a while, or completely crashed and flat later on.

Over the past two weeks, would you say you have spent most of your time feeling energized and wired, mostly flat and drained, or have you been rapidly switching back and forth between these two states every few days?

Over the past two weeks, I would say I've spent most of my time feeling incredibly energized and wired, barely sleeping and racing around with different projects. I've had brief moments where I feel myself starting to crash, but that buzzing, high-energy state has definitely been dominating lately.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets the criteria for Bipolar Affective Disorder, currently in a manic episode without psychotic symptoms (F31.1). Over the past two weeks, the patient has been in a sustained, dominant state of high energy, decreased need for sleep (2-3 hours per night), racing thoughts, and goal-directed hyperactivity. This state has caused significant functional impairment and involved high-risk behaviors (reckless driving, excessive spending). The patient also has a history of a distinct major depressive episode (flat mood, loss of interest, lack of energy lasting weeks), which confirms the bipolar course.
